references.text: Isaiah uses the same imagery of terror, the pit, and a snare that comes upon all inhabitants of the earth: 'Terror and the pit and the snare are upon you, O inhabitant of the earth!' (Isaiah 24:17). The motif of an unavoidable judgment striking the whole earth corresponds with Jesus' words about the snare that will come upon everyone.

Jeremiah uses similar phrases concerning terror, the pit, and a snare over the inhabitants of Moab (Jeremiah 48:43), reflecting the same theme of unavoidable judgment that Jesus applies universally in Luke 21:35.

Ecclesiastes writes that humans do not know their time, 'just as fish are caught in an evil net and birds are caught in a snare' (Ecclesiastes 9:12). The image of the snare (παγίς) suddenly catching corresponds with Jesus' warning about unexpected judgment.

Paul warns that destruction will come suddenly upon those who say, 'Peace and safety,' 'just as labor pains come upon a woman in childbirth, and they will not escape' (1 Thessalonians 5:3). The parallel with Luke 21:35 is clear: an unexpected judgment that strikes everyone from which no one can escape.

The immediate context in Luke 21:34 warns against letting hearts be weighed down by carousing, drunkenness, and the worries of life, so that 'that day' comes unexpectedly like a snare—this provides the direct background for the image of the snare in verse 35.

Isaiah prophesies that the Lord will make the earth desolate and turn it upside down (Isaiah 24:1). The expression 'the face of all the earth' (πρόσωπον πάσης τῆς γῆς) in Luke 21:35 points to a universal judgment that strikes all inhabitants of the earth, as Isaiah describes.

In Revelation 3:10, Christ commends the church in Philadelphia and promises to keep them from 'the hour of trial that is coming on the whole world to test those who dwell on the earth.' The expression 'those who dwell on the earth' and the universal trial closely link this to Luke 21:35.

In Genesis 7:4, God says he will wipe out all living things 'from the face of the earth.' The expression 'the face of the earth' (πρόσωπον τῆς γῆς) is used in a similar way in Luke 21:35 to describe a judgment that strikes universally.

In Luke 17:35–36, Jesus describes how the day of the Son of Man will strike people in everyday situations—one is taken, the other left. This underscores the same theme as in Luke 21:35: judgment comes unexpectedly upon all 'who are on the earth.'
